# An Observation of Ants in the Bathroom

Throughout the bathroom, I notice countless tiny bronze-colored ants scattered across nearly every surface. They crawl along the windowsill, traverse the ceiling overhead, and make their way over the towel, the soap, and the edges of the tub. Their sheer numbers are striking—a restless population occupying the small space with quiet persistence.

These insects belong to the sub-family Formicinae, identifiable by two distinguishing features: a single segment situated behind the thorax and abdomens curved into the shape of a sickle-moon. These anatomical details set them apart and mark their particular place in the natural order.

Though they are commonly described as "social creatures," there is something unsettling in their society. It appears grim and mechanical—a procession of identical pilgrims moving with purpose. Now and then, two of them pause to briefly touch faces, a fleeting moment of contact. More sobering still, some carry their dead clutched in their jaws, transporting the fallen with an eerie sense of duty.

Their reproductive process unfolds in flight. The winged queen mates while airborne, and only afterward does she shed her wings, returning to earth to plant her larvae in the sand. It is a strange and elaborate cycle, hidden from ordinary view.

Meanwhile, the infestation continues. More ants emerge, following the cracks in the tile and tracing the edge of the tub in steady lines. One crawls across the surface of the mirror, and in the reflection it appears doubled—a single ant multiplied, as if to underscore how thoroughly they have claimed this space as their own.

# The Ants in the Bathroom

They come in the early morning, before I have fully woken, threading their dark procession along the grout between the tiles. *Formicidae*—family of the order Hymenoptera, cousins to the wasp and bee. I know this the way one knows any inherited fact, and yet the knowledge does nothing to diminish the strangeness of them, these small punctuation marks moving with such certainty across the white expanse of porcelain.

I have learned to watch them. There is a colony somewhere beneath the house, or in the wall's hidden cavity, and what I see is only the visible thread of a vast and buried enterprise. Each worker is a sterile female, I remember reading—her ovaries stilled, her whole existence given over to labor she will never profit from. She carries crumbs larger than her body. She follows the pheromone trail laid down by others, a chemical scripture written on the air, invisible to me but as legible to her as any road. What looks like wandering is in fact obedience. What looks like chaos is a language.

And so the bathroom becomes a country, and I its idle god, looking down.

I think of cities when I watch them. I think of the morning trains, the human rivers pouring across bridges toward the offices and factories, each body certain of its errand, none pausing to ask who benefits. We too lay down our invisible trails. We too follow. The ant does not question the queen she feeds, that swollen sovereign in her chamber laying egg after egg, ten thousand daughters spun from a single act of mating that happened once, long ago, in a nuptial flight the workers will never know. The queen remembers flight. The workers were born already earthbound, already committed.

Reproduction—that great engine—hums beneath all of it. The colony exists to make more colony. The individual is nothing; the individual is a sentence in service of the paragraph, the paragraph in service of the book that is the species, endlessly rewriting itself. I find this beautiful and I find it terrible, and I am not certain the two feelings can be separated.

One ant has strayed from the line. She circles near the drain, antennae testing the porcelain, and I understand that she is lost—that a worker separated from the trail will sometimes spiral until she dies, following her own scent in a closing ring, a small tragedy of pure geometry. I could help her. I could not help her. I am the size of weather to her, an event without motive she could ever comprehend. This is, I suppose, how I feel about my own dying: that it approaches from a scale I cannot see, indifferent, following laws I did not write.

And still they work. The line reforms. The lost one is not mourned; there is no mourning in a colony, only continuation. Tomorrow there will be ants again, and the day after, each one carrying its fragment toward the dark, and I will stand here in my slippers in the cold morning light, brushing my teeth, watching the small machinery of the world go about its ancient and unhurried business on the floor beneath my feet.

How ordinary. How impossibly strange. That in this room of tile and mirror, this most domestic of spaces, I should find the whole grammar of existence written small—society and sacrifice, the queen and the sterile daughter, the trail and the wandering, the making and the ending—all of it moving, all of it going somewhere, all of it going on.

# Two Winters in Siberia

Antony had never imagined his life would lead him to the frozen wilderness of Siberia. Yet here he was, a young researcher from England, bundled in layers of wool and fur, staring out at an endless expanse of white.

It had been **two** years since he first arrived at the remote weather station. The isolation had changed him. In the beginning, Antony counted the days, marking each one on a battered calendar pinned above his cot. But as the seasons turned, he stopped counting and started living.

Siberia was harsh and unforgiving. The temperatures dropped so low that his breath froze the moment it left his lips. Nights stretched long and dark, broken only by the occasional shimmer of the northern lights dancing across the sky. Antony learned to respect this land, its silence, and its brutal beauty.

His only companion was Dmitri, a weathered local guide who had lived in the region his entire life. Together, the **two** men shared meals of hot soup and black bread, exchanging stories in broken languages. Dmitri taught Antony how to read the weather in the movement of clouds and how to survive when the snowstorms swallowed the world whole.

"You are different now," Dmitri once told him, his eyes crinkling with a knowing smile. "Siberia has become part of you."

Antony realized the old man was right. What had started as a simple assignment had transformed into something deeper. He had discovered a resilience within himself he never knew existed. The vast wilderness had stripped away his fears and taught him patience.

When his contract finally ended, Antony stood at the small airstrip, waiting for the plane that would carry him home. He looked back one last time at the land that had shaped him. **Two** winters in Siberia had given him more than any classroom ever could.

And somehow, he knew he would return.

counterfactuals.output:
# Foraging Behavior in the Genus *Home*

They arrive along the grout-line, that pale meridian between tile and tile, a trail of *Lasius niger* or something like them—I never learned the smaller Latin, only the way they thread the seam beside the tub as if following a river I cannot see.

*The workers are sterile females*, the field guide says, and I think of them here in the steam of my own body's washing, these daughters who will never be mothers, negotiating the drought of porcelain. They move by pheromone, laying down a language of scent behind them, so that each ant is a sentence the next one reads. *Trail fidelity increases with resource quality.* Meaning: they have found something. Meaning: a crumb of my morning has become a pilgrimage.

I have watched one carry a fleck of soap—mistaken sweetness—the whole long white cliff of the baseboard, antenna testing the air the way my grandmother tested bathwater with the inside of her wrist. *Tenderly*, is the unscientific word. It is not tenderness. It is chemistry doing what tenderness only imitates.

Under the sink they have made a country. *Colonies may persist for years*, undisturbed behind the pipes, in the dark municipality of the wall, while above them I brush my teeth and grow older and rinse the day from my face. We are neighbors who will never meet. We share a border and a thirst.

Sometimes I kill them. Let me be honest as a field guide: *a single thumb, applied with pressure.* And the trail, disrupted, panics into confusion—a scattering, a scribble, the pheromone road erased. Then, slowly, the returning. Always the returning. They do not grieve the one I took. They only find another way toward the water, toward the sweetness, toward the small warm evidence that here, in this room where I am most alone, most animal, most naked—

something else is also living, also drinking, also carrying its impossible load home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a richly detailed literary meditation on watching insects invade a bathroom while you take a bath, blending naturalist observation with poetic reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
# Communion in the Small Hours

The water has gone tepid around me, that particular temperature the body stops registering, and I have been still long enough that the room has forgotten I am in it. This is when they come—or rather, this is when I finally see them, having been too loud in my presence before, too much the assumed sovereign of these tiles.

A silverfish emerges first from the seam where the bathtub meets the wall, that dark meridian of caulk gone soft and yellow with years of steam. It moves the way water moves, if water had decided to become an animal—a liquid dart, three tapered filaments trailing behind like the afterthought of its own motion. *Lepisma saccharina*, the sugar-eater, older than the dinosaurs, older than flowers, older than the very concept of wings. It has been running this same errand across bathroom floors since before there were bathrooms, since before there was anything to be clean.

I do not move. The bath has taught me a monastic stillness, and I have become, for once, a good student.

---

Consider what a bathroom is to them. To me it is a room of ablution, of privacy, of the small daily liturgy of getting clean. But to the insect it is a *biome*—a humid gorge, a valley of unexpected water, walls of impossible smoothness broken by the mercy of grout. The condensation on the mirror is a lake. The puddle around the drain is an ocean with a terrible undertow. The whole architecture of my comfort is, to them, weather.

A moth has found the light above the sink and begins its ancient devotion, that helpless spiraling toward brightness that we have never fully understood. The old explanation—that they navigate by the moon and are confused by artificial light—may not even be true; recent watchers suggest they simply try to keep the light *above* them, to orient their backs to the sky, and our bulbs betray this instinct, tumbling them into confusion. There is a whole cosmology in that flutter. The moth is not stupid. The moth is applying a wisdom ten million years old to a circumstance ten decades new. Who among us would fare better, dropped into a world whose rules had silently changed?

---

The steam thins. Through the cracked window comes the evening, and with it a mosquito, thin as a rumor, whining her high electric note. Only the females bite—this too is a kind of poetry, that the blood-hunger belongs to motherhood, that she wants me only because something in her is preparing to become many. She lands on my forearm where it rests along the porcelain lip, and I watch her with a strange tenderness, this delicate machine of need. Her proboscis is not a single needle but a bundle of six, a surgeon's whole kit folded into a filament finer than a hair. She is drilling for the iron that will build her eggs. I am, to her, simply the nearest generosity.

I let her drink a moment before I move. Call it a tithe.

---

Why do we call it *invasion*? The word assumes a border, a sovereignty, a rightful owner pushed upon by trespass. But I am the newcomer here. The silverfish's lineage predates my species by four hundred million years. The house was built on ground that was theirs, of materials that harbor them, in a climate they have colonized more thoroughly than any empire dreamed. They do not invade the bathroom. They *are* the bathroom, in some deeper sense—its true and permanent residents—and I am the seasonal flood, the strange warm giant who comes at evening, displaces the water, and leaves.

There is a humility available in this, if I am willing to take it. The bath strips me of everything—clothes, posture, the day's accumulated importance. And here, in this reduced and dripping state, I am joined by the small persistent life that never left, that runs its errands through the walls whether I bathe or work or sleep or die. They will be here after. They were here before. My cleanliness is a brief performance in a theater they have always owned.

---

A spider, meanwhile, has strung her architecture in the high corner where two walls and the ceiling meet, that geometric intimacy no broom of mine has troubled in months. She is patient in the way I am only ever pretending to be. The moth, still drunk on light, drifts too near, and I feel the whole room hold its breath—do I intervene? Do I let the drama complete itself? This is the oldest transaction, older than mercy, older than cruelty, the simple mathematics of one life converting into another. I choose, this time, to do nothing, which is itself a choice, and the moth, by some grace or luck, veers off, and the web trembles with a hunger unfulfilled.

The water is cold now. Truly cold. My fingers have pruned into little topographies, and the light through the window has gone the blue of endings.

---

I could tell you I learned something profound in that tepid hour—that the insects taught me my smallness, or the world's persistence, or the thin membrane between my ordered life and the teeming indifference just behind the tiles. All of that is true and all of it is too neat.

What I actually felt was simpler and harder to hold: a kinship without sentiment. We were all of us in that room doing the same thing, which is the only thing anything does—seeking water, seeking warmth, seeking the next hour of being alive. The silverfish, the moth, the mosquito heavy now with my blood, the patient spider, and the pale animal gone cold in the bath, watching. Not master and pest. Not host and vermin. Just a handful of hungers sharing a humid room at the end of a day, each certain of its own centrality, each wrong, each beautiful in its wrongness.

I rise at last, and the water sheets off me, and the whole small nation scatters into its cracks and seams and shadows. The room becomes mine again, briefly, provisionally. I pull the plug and listen to my private ocean drain away into pipes that are, I know, another country entirely—another dark and dripping world, populated, patient, indifferent, and utterly, teemingly alive.

I turn off the light. I give them back their bathroom. I go to bed above them, and they resume their ancient errands, and the house holds us all in its plaster and its silence, the great and the small, the temporary and the eternal, breathing together in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# Formic

The field guide says: *In *Tapinoma sessile*, the odorous house ant, workers emit a coconut-rotten scent when crushed.* I have crushed a hundred against porcelain and smelled nothing but my own panic, that sweet decay of wanting a clean thing kept clean.

They come up through the grout like thoughts I didn't invite, a black seam unstitching itself along the tub's white lip, each body a comma in a sentence with no verb, no end. *Foraging trails are laid via pheromone*, the guide insists, *a chemical script legible only to the colony*—and so they read the invisible cursive of the ant before them, nose to abdomen, a rosary of hunger telling itself across the cold enamel horizon.

Here, on the soap dish, one has drowned in a bead of water, legs curled inward like an eyelash, like a punctuation mark erased. The others do not mourn. *The dead are borne to a midden*, the field guide notes, *identified by oleic acid, the odor of decomposition*—so death is only another smell to follow, a directive. They lift their sister and carry her out along the same road they came, the corpse a dark seed passed hand to hand, mouth to mouth, into the dark.

And once a year, the winged ones. *Nuptial flight occurs when temperature and humidity align*, the guide says, dry as chalk. But there is nothing dry in it: the alates boil up from the drain in their brief inheritance of wings, males dying the instant after, spent match-heads, while the queen tears her own wings off like wet paper and begins. Begins the tunneling, the swallowing of her own flight muscles for protein, the laying, the founding of a nation in the wall behind my mirror.

*A single colony may contain multiple queens*, the guide concludes, *and thus may persist indefinitely.* Indefinitely. I turn off the light. In the dark they continue, a black arithmetic summing and summing across the tile, patient as rust, ancient as the salt in blood—doing what they have always done beneath our brief and shining rooms: carrying the small dead home, reading the sweet script of the world, unspooling their one long sentence toward whatever it is that ants believe in, which is only more ants, forever, and the warm damp seam of everything we cannot keep out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental nonfiction that closely observes a small colony of ants in a domestic setting, using metaphors of pilgrimage, royalty, and religion.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Communicants

*An observation, conducted over eleven days, of a colony of pavement ants established in the seam between countertop and backsplash, kitchen, north-facing.*

---

**Day One.**

They arrive the way rumor arrives—not all at once but as a thing that was already true before you noticed it. One ant, then the suggestion of another, then the certainty of a third. By evening there is a line, and a line is a scripture: it insists on being read left to right, or right to left, depending on which way hunger points.

I have left a single crumb of shortbread near the toaster. I did not mean to. This is how most theologies begin—with an accident that later gets described as providence.

---

**Day Two.**

The pilgrims have found the crumb.

I use the word *pilgrim* and I mean it precisely. Each ant travels an impossible distance—a countertop is, to them, a continent, and I am the weather that crosses it—toward a site made holy by the promise of return. They touch the shortbread with their faces. They do not eat so much as *venerate*, taking a particle, turning, carrying the relic home along the pilgrim road their sisters have consecrated with scent.

Because that is the secret the guidebooks won't tell you about pilgrimage: the destination is never the point. The *route* is the point. They lay down invisible chemical psalms, and each ant that follows sings the same note a little louder, until the trail is a hymn any of them can find in the dark.

---

**Day Three.**

I have been calling them *she*, and I am right to. The travelers are all daughters. Somewhere below the visible world—inside the wall, in a warm dark I will never be permitted to enter—there is a Queen.

I never see her. This is the condition of her queenship. She is the still point that makes all the motion mean something. Every crumb hauled back through the seam is tribute to a monarch none of the couriers have looked upon, will ever look upon, could survive looking upon. They are loyal to an absence. They have organized their entire brief lives around a body they take on faith.

I find this more coherent than most of what I believe.

---

**Day Four.**

An experiment, cruel and small:

I place my fingertip across the trail. I break the line. I want to see the crisis of the interrupted faithful.

The result is theater. The ants at the severed edge stop—not gracefully—and begin a frantic circling, antennae thrashing the empty air where the scripture used to be. They have lost the text. A pilgrim without her road is not lost in the way I am lost; she is *unmade*, returned to raw searching, to the animal panic that precedes all religion.

Then one finds the thread again. Touches the psalm. And the certainty flows back into her like a current, and she resumes, and the others resume behind her, and the small apocalypse is over. Forty seconds, perhaps. In their time-signature, a dark age. A wandering in a wilderness. A book of a faith recovered.

I lift my finger. I feel like a bad god, which is the only honest kind.

---

**Day Six.**

I skipped a day. I want to be truthful about my own lapses of attention, since I am demanding such devotion from them.

Today: rain outside, and inside a great multiplication. The trail has thickened into a nave, a central aisle down which the congregation moves in two directions at once—the empty-handed going, the burdened returning—and they pass each other constantly, and each passing is a sacrament.

They touch. Every single time. Antenna to antenna, a brush, a benediction, gone. This is how they know each other: not by faces but by *chemistry*, by the shared smell of the same mother, the same nest, the same god. To be recognized is to be smelled and found familial. Every greeting is a confession—*I am of the Queen, are you of the Queen*—and every answering touch is absolution: *you are, go in peace, the crumb awaits.*

I have shaken hands at funerals with less meaning in it.

---

**Day Seven.**

The shortbread is gone. Not moved—*transubstantiated*. Converted particle by particle into ant, into egg, into the continuance of the hidden Queen. The relic has been wholly consumed by its own veneration, which is what relics are for.

For a few hours the trail persists anyway. The pilgrims arrive at the empty site and mill in the disappointment of the faithful who have reached the shrine and found the saint's bones already dust. Faith outlives its object. It always does. That's how you know it was faith and not merely appetite.

By nightfall the scent-psalm, unrefreshed, has begun to evaporate. The road is un-writing itself. Fewer come. Then fewer.

---

**Day Nine.**

Almost none now. One straggler, a late pilgrim arriving at a cathedral already deconsecrated, walking the ghost of a route the others have forgotten. She casts about. She finds nothing. She turns for home along a trail so faint it must be more memory than smell.

I want to leave another crumb for her. I want to be a merciful weather. I understand suddenly why gods intervene—not from love but from the unbearable spectacle of devotion going unanswered.

I do not leave the crumb. An observer who feeds the observed is no longer observing; she is writing scripture herself, authoring the very providence she claims to record. I keep my hands off the continent.

---

**Day Eleven.**

Nothing. The seam is just a seam. The countertop is just a plain.

But I know now what I did not know eleven days ago: that below my floor, inside my wall, in a warmth I heat and pay for and cannot visit, the Queen persists. She was fed. The tribute reached her. The pilgrimage, however invisible its terminus, *arrived*. Somewhere in the dark a body I will never see is heavy with the future, made fat on shortbread carried grain by grain across a world by daughters who died believing in a mother they never met, along roads they wrote in a language made of longing.

I clean the counter. I wipe away the last of the trail, the last chemical verse, the final line of a testament.

And I find, doing it, that I am being careful. That I am—God help me—*reverent.*

That the smallest church I have ever entered was in my own kitchen, and I was too large to fit through its door, and the congregation prayed anyway, and their prayers were answered, and mine, as usual, were not.

counterfactuals.output: They come in a punctuated line across the cold porcelain, each one a small dark theorem: the first ant, mandibles working, carries a crumb larger than her head, for an ant can lift twenty times her own weight and never once considers it a burden; the second pauses at the lip of the sink, antennae testing the air in that language of pheromones by which the colony thinks as a single distributed mind, no queen commanding, only the murmured chemistry of consensus; the third traverses the spine of a paperback left splayed beside the faucet, *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, and I watch her cross the word *solitude* though she has never in her life been alone, has never known a self apart from the sisterhood that raised her, for every worker is female, sterile, ancient—ants have farmed and warred and buried their dead for a hundred million years, longer than the flowers; the fourth drowns, briefly, in a bead of water and does not drown, because her body is hydrophobic and the droplet becomes a lens through which I see the tiled world curved and enormous; and the fifth simply stops at the edge of the mirror, meeting the other fifth, the reflected one, and I think how strange to be a creature who cannot recognize herself, and stranger still to be the one who can, standing here at two in the morning in my own reflection, watching these small industrious punctuation marks spell out a sentence I will never be able to read.
